title: Present Simple Tense
subtitle: For habits, routines and facts
tip: Use the base verb. Add -s/-es for he, she, it.

items.point: Use it for things you do regularly or facts that are always true.
items.example: I go to work every day.

items.point: For he, she, it - add -s or -es to the verb.
Make questions with do / does.
Make negatives with do not / does not.

title: Present Continuous
subtitle: For actions happening right now
tip: am / is / are + verb-ing.

items.point: Use it for something happening at this moment.
items.example: I am reading a book now.

items.point: Use am with I, is with he/she/it, are with you/we/they.
Also for temporary situations these days.
items.example: She is studying for her exam this week.

items.point: Question: put am/is/are first.

title: Past Simple Tense
subtitle: For finished actions in the past
tip: Add -ed to regular verbs; learn irregular ones.

items.point: Use it for actions that finished in the past.
Regular verbs add -ed.
Many common verbs are irregular - learn them.
Questions and negatives use did.
items.example: Did you call him? / I did not see it.

title: Future: will and going to
subtitle: For actions in the future
tip: will = decide now; going to = already planned.

items.point: Use will for a decision made right now or a promise.
items.example: I will help you with that.

items.point: Use going to for plans you already decided.
items.example: We are going to travel next month.

items.point: Will is also used for predictions.
Question: Will you...? / Are you going to...?

title: Articles: a, an, the
subtitle: Small words before nouns
tip: a/an = one, any; the = a specific one.

items.point: Use a before a consonant sound.
Use an before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u).
Use the when both people know which one.
Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.
items.example: I like music. / Dogs are friendly.

title: Sentence Order: Subject-Verb-Object
subtitle: How to build a basic sentence
tip: English usually follows Subject + Verb + Object.

items.point: The subject does the action, then the verb, then the object.
Keep this order in most sentences.
Add time/place usually at the end.
items.example: We play cricket in the park.

items.point: Do not drop the subject.

title: Question Words
subtitle: How to ask for information
tip: What, Where, When, Who, Why, Which, Whose, How.

items.point: What asks about a thing.
Where asks about a place.
When asks about time.
Why asks for a reason; How asks about manner.
items.example: Why are you late? / How are you?

title: Plural Nouns
subtitle: Talking about more than one
tip: Usually add -s; sometimes -es or a special form.

items.point: Add -s to most nouns.
Add -es after s, x, ch, sh.
Some nouns change completely (irregular).
Some nouns stay the same.

title: Present Perfect
subtitle: Past action connected to now
tip: have / has + past participle (third form).

items.point: Use it for a past action with a result now, no exact time.
Use has with he, she, it.
Use it for experiences in your life.
Use 'for' and 'since' for duration.
items.example: I have lived here for five years.

title: Past Continuous
subtitle: An action in progress in the past
tip: was / were + verb-ing.

items.point: Use it for an action happening at a moment in the past.
items.example: I was watching TV at 8 pm.

items.point: Often used with past simple for interruption.
items.example: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

items.point: Use was with I/he/she/it, were with you/we/they.
Sets the background of a story.
items.example: The sun was shining and birds were singing.

title: Comparatives and Superlatives
subtitle: Comparing things
tip: -er / more for two; -est / most for the top.

items.point: Short words add -er to compare two things.
items.example: This box is bigger than that one.

items.point: Long words use 'more'.
items.example: This book is more interesting than that one.

items.point: For the highest, add -est or use 'most'.
items.example: He is the tallest boy in the class.

items.point: Some are irregular.
items.example: good -> better -> best, bad -> worse -> worst

title: Modals: can, could
subtitle: Ability and polite requests
tip: can = present ability; could = past or polite.

items.point: Use can for present ability.
Use could for past ability.
items.example: When I was young, I could run fast.

items.point: Use could for polite requests.
Negative: cannot / could not.

title: Modals: should, must, have to
subtitle: Advice and obligation
tip: should = advice; must / have to = necessary.

items.point: Use should to give advice.
Use must for strong necessity or rules.
Have to shows necessity from outside.
items.example: I have to finish this today.

items.point: Should not / must not for what is wrong.

title: Prepositions of Time: in, on, at
subtitle: When something happens
tip: at = time, on = day/date, in = month/year.

items.point: Use at for exact times.
Use on for days and dates.
items.example: I will see you on Monday.

items.point: Use in for months, years, and long periods.
Use in for parts of the day (except night).
items.example: I study in the morning. / at night.

title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
subtitle: many, much, some, any
tip: many for countable; much for uncountable.

items.point: Countable nouns can be counted; use many.
items.example: How many books do you have?

items.point: Uncountable nouns cannot be counted; use much.
items.example: How much water do you want?

items.point: Use some in positive sentences.
Use any in questions and negatives.
items.example: Do you have any sugar? / I don't have any.

title: Adverbs of Frequency
subtitle: How often you do things
tip: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

items.point: They tell how often something happens.
Put them before the main verb.
But after the verb 'be'.
Never already means 'not', so don't add 'not'.

title: Present Perfect Continuous
subtitle: How long an action has continued
tip: have / has been + verb-ing.

items.point: Use it for an action that started in the past and is still going.
items.example: I have been working here for two years.

items.point: It focuses on the length of the activity.
items.example: She has been studying since morning.

items.point: Often answers 'how long?'.
items.example: How long have you been waiting?

items.point: Compare with present perfect (result vs duration).
items.example: I have read the book. / I have been reading all day.

title: Past Perfect
subtitle: The earlier of two past actions
tip: had + past participle.

items.point: Use it for an action that happened before another past action.
items.example: The train had left before I reached the station.

items.point: It makes the order of past events clear.
items.example: She had finished dinner when I arrived.

items.point: Often used with 'before', 'after', 'by the time'.
items.example: By the time we came, the show had started.

items.point: Negative: had not.
items.example: I had not seen that film before.

title: Conditionals (If sentences)
subtitle: Talking about possibilities
tip: Zero, First, Second, Third - different uses.

items.point: Zero: general truths. If + present, present.
items.example: If you heat ice, it melts.

items.point: First: real future. If + present, will.
items.example: If it rains, I will stay home.

items.point: Second: unreal now. If + past, would.
items.example: If I had money, I would travel.

items.point: Third: unreal past. If + had + past participle, would have.
items.example: If I had studied, I would have passed.

title: Passive Voice
subtitle: When the action matters, not the doer
tip: be + past participle.

items.point: Use it when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
Form: subject + be + past participle.
Add 'by' to mention the doer.
items.example: The cake was made by my mother.

items.point: Common in news and formal writing.
items.example: A new bridge is being built.

title: Reported Speech
subtitle: Telling what someone said
tip: Move the tense one step back.

items.point: Change the tense back when reporting.
items.example: He said, 'I am tired.' -> He said he was tired.

items.point: Present becomes past.
items.example: 'I work here.' -> She said she worked there.

items.point: Change time and place words too.
Questions use if/whether or a question word.
items.example: He asked if I was coming.

title: Relative Clauses
subtitle: Adding info with who, which, that
tip: who = people, which = things, that = both.

items.point: Use who for people.
items.example: The man who called you is my uncle.

items.point: Use which for things.
items.example: The phone which I bought is new.

items.point: Use that for people or things (informal).
items.example: The book that you gave me is great.

items.point: Use where for places, whose for possession.
items.example: This is the house where I grew up.

title: Gerunds and Infinitives
subtitle: -ing vs to + verb
tip: Some verbs take -ing, some take 'to'.

items.point: A gerund is verb + ing used as a noun.
After some verbs use the gerund (enjoy, avoid, finish).
After some verbs use the infinitive (want, decide, hope).
After prepositions, use the gerund.

title: Future Continuous and Perfect
subtitle: Advanced future forms
tip: will be + -ing / will have + past participle.

items.point: Future continuous: an action in progress in the future.
items.example: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Delhi.

items.point: Future perfect: an action finished before a future time.
items.example: By next year, I will have completed my course.

items.point: Use them to sound fluent and precise.
items.example: She will be waiting for you.

items.point: Question form keeps 'will' first.
items.example: Will you be joining us tonight?

title: Pronouns
subtitle: Words that replace nouns
tip: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.

items.point: Use a pronoun instead of repeating a name.
items.example: Ravi is my friend. He is kind.

items.point: Subject pronouns do the action.
Object pronouns receive the action.
Possessive pronouns show belonging.

title: There is / There are
subtitle: Saying something exists
tip: there is + singular; there are + plural.

items.point: Use 'there is' for one thing.
items.example: There is a book on the table.

items.point: Use 'there are' for many things.
Question: Is there...? / Are there...?
Negative: there isn't / there aren't.

title: Conjunctions
subtitle: Joining words: and, but, because
tip: Connect ideas smoothly.

items.point: Use 'and' to add.
Use 'but' to show contrast.
Use 'because' to give a reason.
Use 'so' to show a result.
items.example: It rained, so we stayed home.

title: Question Tags
subtitle: Adding a mini-question at the end
tip: positive sentence -> negative tag.

items.point: Add a short question to confirm.
Positive sentence takes a negative tag.
items.example: She is a doctor, isn't she?

items.point: Negative sentence takes a positive tag.
Match the helping verb.

title: Used to
subtitle: Talking about past habits
tip: used to + base verb.

items.point: Use 'used to' for something you did regularly in the past.
items.example: I used to play cricket every day.

items.point: It shows the habit has stopped now.
items.example: She used to smoke, but she quit.

items.point: Question: Did you use to...?
items.example: Did you use to live here?

items.point: Do not confuse with 'be used to' (be familiar with).
items.example: I am used to the noise now.

title: So and Such
subtitle: Making words stronger
tip: so + adjective; such + (a) noun.

items.point: Use 'so' before an adjective or adverb.
Use 'such' before a noun phrase.
items.example: It was such a good film.

items.point: With a singular noun, add 'a/an'.
items.example: She is such an intelligent girl.

items.point: They add emphasis to your feelings.
